pages.text: Mirtunjaya Goswami 1mo Report this comment Ilya Strebulaev It’s funny the more we “democratized” entrepreneurship, the rarer the miracles became. In 1998, a startup had a 6% shot at becoming a unicorn; by 2021, that fell below 1%. We built faster funding pipelines, bigger venture funds, and infinite pitch decks yet the conversion rate to greatness collapsed. Perhaps the market didn’t get more competitive; it just got more crowded with belief. Like Reply 3 Reactions 4 Reactions Christian Pobbig 4w Report this comment The data you’ve shared raises an interesting question: are we likely to see a resurgence in unicorn probabilities, or has the startup landscape fundamentally shifted to favour smaller exits over time? Like Reply 1 Reaction Marina L. 1mo [...] While the absolute number of unicorns has increased in recent years, the probability for any individual startup to reach unicorn status has become increasingly rare. Our analysis tracks the percentage of startups that received first VC funding in a specific year that later reached unicorn status: • 1998 had the highest probability (6.2%) of startups becoming unicorns • While 2021 saw the most new unicorns (353), the probability of becoming one was low (0.65%) After peaking in the late 1990s, unicorn probability dropped in the early 2000s The rates for recent years are biased downward since it typically takes several years after initial funding for startups to reach unicorn status. Thank you to the Stanford University Graduate School of Business Venture Capital Initiative for support.

pages.title: VC Due Diligence Math: 3,226 Startups per Outlier | Alex Samson
pages.text: ## Why 3,226 applications# We all know that 90% of startups fail. In April 2024, 60x angel investor and LP Rem Darbinyan at STAN's webinar added that another 6.9% become self-sustaining businesses that don't deliver the returns VCs need to cover failures. So basically, 3.1% of the 1% of invested startups outperform. Donut chart of startup outcomes: 90% fail, 6.9% become self-sustaining, 3% exit through IPO or M&A, 0.1% become unicorns This means a VC has to review 3,226 startup applications per year (1 ÷ (1% × 3.1%)) to get a chance at one outlier. [...] Key numbers: 1% of deal flow gets funded, 3.1% of funded startups outperform, so one outlier takes about 3,226 applications and 323 due diligences a year. The first week at the VC Lab Venture Institute gave me two key insights: 1. Seek opportunities for 10-100x returns, rather than just investing in any new tech business that can earn a profit or be acquired with at least 2x returns. 2. 1% of startups in deal flow get funded, which requires reviewing 1,000 applications to make 10 investments per year. Out of 500 applications, about 50 make it to a first call, 10 to due diligence, and one gets funded. ## Why 3,226 applications#

pages.text: Understanding why startups fail is a survival skill. In this article, we’ll break down the latest failure rates, the most common reasons behind them, and what today’s founders can learn to avoid becoming another statistic. ## Startup Failure Statistics 9 out of 10 startups fail (source: Startup Genome - the 2019 report claims 11 out of 12 fail). 7.5 out of 10 venture-backed startups fail (source: Shikhar Ghosh). 2 out of 10 new businesses fail in the first year of operations (source: Bureau of Labor). Only 1% of startups become unicorn firms like Uber, Airbnb, Slack, Stripe, and Docker (source: CB Insights). The success percentage for first-time founders is 18% (source: Exploding Topics). [...] This means their failure rates would be lower than those of early-stage startups. Harvard Business School lecturer Shikhar Ghosh says in a WSJ article that 75% of venture-backed companies never return cash to investors and in 30-40% of the cases, investors lose their initial investment (he works with a dataset of 2000 venture-backed startups). That said, only 0.05% of startups get VC funding (Source: Fundable), so this statistic does not apply to the vast majority of new businesses, especially if they are in the early idea stage. ### Failure Rates of All Startups: Early-stage (idea stage) startups bear the highest risk and failure rates. It’s hard to claim accuracy about failure rate statistics for those kinds of projects because a large chunk fly below the radar.

pages.title: Founder First, Unicorn Second: Fixing the Broken Model of Venture Capital
pages.publishedDateEvidence: Publisher's schema.org datePublished (JSON-LD), read from the page itself
pages.text: ## The Power Law Reality — And Why It Persists The Power Law dominates venture capital. Recent Y Combinator stats reveal 75% of returns come from 5% of investments. A 2023 Pitchbook analysis found only 1.3% of venture-backed startups reach valuations above $1 billion. This model emerged when Silicon Valley legends like Intel and Apple flourished from significant bets, but it persists due to subtle biases and entrenched incentives. Consider investor ego. A big win is intoxicating, and investors become addicted to it. Herd mentality makes VCs pile onto trendy sectors, amplifying hype but ignoring quieter opportunities. Rarely discussed is the fear among them—fear of missing the next Airbnb—even though chasing that fear blinds them to profitable, stable ventures. [...] "But what about the next Google or Facebook?" These outliers represent less than 0.1% of startups. Building a system around extreme ones makes little sense for the ecosystem. Many tech giants like Microsoft and Apple achieved scale with modest initial investment—Microsoft's only venture round was $1 million from David Marquardt in 1981. A balanced approach doesn't eliminate moonshot potential; it doesn't sacrifice the other 99.9% of companies to pursue it. "Don't traditional VCs provide valuable expertise and connections?"

analysis.answer: CB Insights' 2018 venture capital funnel analysis found the odds of becoming a unicorn were about 1% (1.07%), with 12 companies reaching that status [1]. The 1% figure is a rough approximation that varies by dataset and cohort: a LinkedIn post by Ilya Strebulaev (a comment on it) states a startup had about a 6% chance of becoming a unicorn in 1998, falling below 1% by 2021 [2]. The claim of exactly 1% is therefore not precise; the origins support 'about 1%' or 'around or below 1%' rather than a fixed 'only 1%' [2] [1].
